newsitem.title: FRANCE: CARREFOUR MOVE ON RIVAL FUELS BID FEVER.
newsitem.headline: CARREFOUR MOVE ON RIVAL FUELS BID FEVER.

text.p: The acquisition by France's largest retailer Carrefour of a big stake in the company controlling the Cora hypermarkets chain on Thursday fanned rampant bid speculation in the French retail sector.
Retail shares jumped as investors anticipated more mergers between chains operating superstores that are intent on securing a strong position in the rapidly consolidating industry.
France's minister for small business, Jean-Pierre Raffarin, encouraged the speculation with an interview in the newspaper Le Figaro in which he said he expected further consolidation.
"Other developments of this type are likely since the French hypermarket sector has reached full capacity, and companies want to become stronger to develop on a global scale," he said.

Raffarin was the author of a law enacted this year that inadvertently prompted the merger activity. In a bid to protect small shops and city centres from the overwhelming competition presented by suburban superstores, he drafted a bill making it harder for big stores to open outlets or extend existing ones.
Private hypermarkets group Auchan said the law was the main factor behind its hostile bid in the summer for Docks de France.
The three largest hypermarkets groups in France are Carrefour and privately owned Leclerc and Intermarche.

Carrefour, which has expanded rapidly overseas and now has more stores outside France, had been viewed as not needing to reinforce its domestic position. But the group on Wednesday said it bought 33 percent of GMB, the holding firm of the Cora chain.

A spokesman for Carrefour said the two companies had geographically complementary activities. Carrefour's 117 stores are distributed throughout central and southeastern France, while Cora's 55 stores are concentrated in the northeast and in Belgium. Cora holds 41 percent of Belgian group Louis Delhaize.
"There's also a common culture, as Cora was formerly a Carrefour subsidiary," the spokesman told Reuters.
Members of the Bouriez family -- though not Cora chairman Philippe Bouriez -- approached Carrefour about a deal.
The Carrefour spokesman said they "considered that Cora's future development had better chances within the framework of an alliance with Carrefour. We thought about it and told them yes."

He said Carrefour had no immediate plan to raise the stake. But one Paris brokerage said it thought Carrefour may seek to buy Cora's hypermarkets and sell its Match supermarkets chain to Comptoirs Modernes , another French retailer.
Shares in the most frequently cited takeover target, Casino, closed up 4.2 percent at 246 francs on Thursday on top of Wednesday's 2.1 percent rise.
Shares in its rumoured suitor, Promodes, were 0.4 percent lower at 1,386 francs after falling 1.7 percent on Wednesday.
Promodes and Casino are ranked fourth and sixth, respectively, in terms of sales.

"They trail behind in terms of size. Promodes lacks the essential critical mass on the French market," said Frederic Genevrier, an analyst at BZW bourse. He said he believed Promodes would seek to acquire Casino's hypermarkets activities.
Promodes and Casino declined to comment on Thursday but they have dropped hints that have sustained the bid speculation.

Promodes chairman Paul-Louis Halley in October said his family could envisage reducing its holding in the company below 30 percent, and he said he expected the industry to consolidate to around five big food-retailing groups.
Holding company Euris, which owns 33 percent of Casino, said in October it did not rule out a retail alliance for Casino.
